extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of trigonometry, surveying, and algebraic geometry (mathematics students, surveyors, geometers)
extracted.subtask_short: trigonometric surveying problems and reciprocal polars
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of trigonometric surveying problem methods (three-station height, distances to remote objects, inaccessible-object separation), an algebraic method for all cubic roots, and a detailed development of the sphero-polar reciprocal of second-degree surfaces with many special-case properties. Includes solution formulas, logarithmic solution procedures, and geometric/algebraic conditions and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Height from three angles of elevation (three stations in a straight line)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the height of an object from angles of elevation taken on a horizontal plane at three given stations in a straight line (not in the direction of the object). Denote the angles at the three stations by a, β, γ and inter-station distances by CK, KD etc.; let AO be perpendicular (height sought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive lengths AC = x cosec a, AK = x cosec β, AD = x cosec γ and reduce to an equation (18) of the form (1+X)x^2 = f (where X relates to interstation ratios). Use the general trigonometric identity 8 sin(A+B) sin(A−B) = ... to reduce. Depending on sign relations between a, β, γ, three distinct substitution/case forms are given: X = tan^2 θ (equations (19),(20)), X = sec^2 θ (equations (21),(22)), X = sin^2 θ (equations (23),(24)). Solve the resulting equations via logarithms as shown (explicit log-forms (19)–(24)). An explicit numeric example is worked through (using the formulas (23),(24)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distances from station to three remote objects given mutual distances and subtended angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the mutual distances of three remote objects P,Q,R (RQ=a, FQ=b, PR=c) and the angles they subtend at a station S (angles at the triangle PQR are A,B,C), find the distances SP, SQ, SR from S to each object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce auxiliary angles and notations (RPS ± RQS = 2w ± 2δ, etc.) to express sines and tangents of sums/differences. Obtain relations of the form sin a sin A / (sin(w+δ)sin B sin C) etc., and reduce to equations (25)–(29). Solve for h (a ratio) via log equation (25) and for θ (an angle) via (26) (log tan relation). Use the sign/case discussion: if h>1 and tan m positive, tan θ negative, etc. Final distances given by log expressions (27)–(29). An explicit numerical example illustrates the full computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance between two inaccessible objects using a known baseline and observed angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a known baseline AB in the observer's plane and observed angles to inaccessible objects C and D from A and B, find the distance CD between those two inaccessible objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the angular relationships (angles at A,B,C,D expressed as a, β, γ, etc.), derive tangent relations and sine products as in earlier problems. The solution reduces to logarithmic formulas: log A = combination of logs of sines/cosecs (30), log tan δ = log(1−A) + log tan m − log(1 + A) (31), and log CD given by (32). Use the stated substitutions and sign rules analogous to previous problems; the section includes the full derivation and indicates how students may adapt for other station positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: New simple process for determining all three roots of a cubic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: A method to determine all three roots of a cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0 by first finding one real root r (e.g., by Horner's method), shifting roots by r, and obtaining remaining parameters a and β directly from transformed coefficients without solving the quadratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original cubic has roots r1, r2, r3 with one root r known, consider roots diminished by r and use transformed coefficients to compute a and β from linear combinations of coefficients (provided in the text). The method avoids solving the resulting quadratic by algebraic extraction of a and β; signs of discriminant (a^2 − 4β) determine whether the remaining two roots are real or complex. A worked numeric example demonstrates Horner iteration and the subsequent algebraic steps to obtain all three roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of reciprocal polar surface (director = sphere): method
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a director sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1 and a general quadratic surface A x^2 + k y^2 + A' z^2 + 2i B yz + ... + 2(Cx + C'y + C''z) + E = 0, find the equation of the surface reciprocal (sphero-polar reciprocal) to the given surface with respect to the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let (α,β,γ) be a point on the given surface and (x',y',z') its reciprocal point. Write the polar plane of (α,β,γ) with respect to the director sphere (equation (a)) and the tangent plane to the given surface at (α,β,γ) (equation labelled xxiii). Equate these two planes and eliminate α,β,γ to obtain the reciprocal surface equation (2) (explicit coefficient expressions in terms of the original surface coefficients). The text gives the explicit expansion (2') with coefficients expressed immediately in terms of those of the reciprocal surface (1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: Ai = 0 ⇒ axis parallel to a side of asymptotic cone (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ai = 0 (for a coefficient in the reciprocal-surface equation), then the axis of x is parallel to a side of the asymptotic cone of the other reciprocal surface; conversely, a plane drawn through the centre of the director perpendicular to a line through the centre parallel to such a side will touch the other surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is deduced from the coefficient relations in the reciprocal equation (see equations (18), No. XXII). The text states the geometric consequence and the converse explicitly: pole/plane incidence relations with respect to the surfaces and the director. Use these conditions to detect tangency relations between reciprocal surfaces and corresponding asymptotic cones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: Bi = 0 ⇒ axes y and z parallel to principal axes (and pole-plane consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Bi = 0 the axes of y and z are parallel to two of the principal axes of the reciprocal surface; further coefficient conditions give that poles of corresponding coordinate planes lie within those planes, with reciprocal geometric consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Via equations (16) and (17), Bi = 0 implies other coefficient vanishing (B'*=0, etc.), producing the pole/plane relations: the pole of the plane of yz lies in that plane and similarly for other coordinate planes. The converse is also given: if two perpendicular planes through the director intersect these pole relations, corresponding principal axes of the polar surface will be respectively perpendicular to those planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: Ci = 0 ⇒ centre on coordinate plane and diametral plane passes through origin
rubrics_metrics.description: When Ci = 0 (one of the linear coefficient sets), the centre of the given surface lies on the specified coordinate plane (e.g., plane yz); the diametral plane of the reciprocal surface which bisects chords parallel to the axis of x passes through the origin, with reciprocal statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of equations (19), No. XXII. Use these vanishing linear coefficients to deduce location of centres and diametral planes; conversely, the stated geometric constructions imply the coefficient conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: Ei = 0 ⇒ centre at infinity and reciprocal passes through origin (paraboloid case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ei = 0 then the centre of the given surface is at infinity and the reciprocal surface passes through the origin; conversely, when one of the reciprocal surfaces is a paraboloid the other passes through the centre of the director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From equations (19), No. XXII; the text explicitly notes that Ei = 0 yields the paraboloid reciprocity and the passage through the origin. This provides an algebraic test for paraboloid behaviour and reciprocal inclusion of the director centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal surfaces with axes aligned to principal axes: simplifications and sphere/paraboloid special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When coordinates are chosen along principal axes of the given surface (so B = B' = B'' = 0), many terms vanish and the reciprocal equation simplifies (see (6) and (7)). Special subcases (C=0, C'=0, C''=0, etc.) produce principal-axis alignment, sphere reciprocals, or paraboloid reciprocal outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With B=0 the reciprocal coefficients take simpler forms (equation (7)). Further specializations (C=0 etc.) are discussed: e.g., if C= C' = C'' = 0 and axes equal the reciprocal surface becomes a sphere with centres collinear; if centre of director lies on the given surface the reciprocal is a paraboloid. The text gives the explicit simplified reciprocal forms and consequent geometric interpretations about parallelism and proportional axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General method for reciprocal polar with an arbitrary second-degree director
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the polar reciprocal of a given second-degree surface with respect to any given second-degree director (not necessarily a sphere), equate the tangent plane of the given surface at a point with the polar plane of that point with respect to the director and eliminate point coordinates to obtain the reciprocal equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text (section XLVIII) gives the director and given surface general forms, writes the tangent plane of the given surface and the polar plane with respect to the director, equates coefficients, and after elimination obtains a general reciprocal equation (displayed as long multiline expression). Special simplifications for central directors (setting certain Q, R, T coefficients to standard values) are given, plus the resulting simplified form (T). Use the provided template to compute reciprocals for arbitrary quadratic directors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorems and special-case consequences for central/director-paraboloid cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of theorems for the central-director or paraboloid-director special cases: e.g., when the director is central many simplifications occur (Q=Q'=Q''=0 etc.), polar plane of the origin has explicit linear form, diametral plane correspondences, tangent/polar coincidences and conditions for intersection in planes are deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates several numbered results (e.g., if the director is central then the linear part can be written as −2E*(...)+E1 and the polar plane of the origin follows). It further lists many geometric consequences: common tangent planes imply passage through points of contact; developable surfaces circumscribed to director and one reciprocal force the other to pass through contact curves; conditions linking asymptotic cones, principal axes, and paraboloid status are provided. Use these as algebraic-to-geometric translation rules when analyzing reciprocal pairs under these special directors.
